title: The Double Diamond, Design Council
text:
## The Double Diamond

The Double Diamond is a visual model of the design and innovation process developed by the UK Design Council in 2003 and 2005. It offers a simple way to describe the steps taken in any design and innovation project, irrespective of the methods and tools used. The model is built from two diamonds that each represent a movement from divergent thinking (exploring an issue widely) to convergent thinking (taking focused action).

## The Four Phases

Discover: the first half of the first diamond. It is about understanding rather than assuming. Teams engage with and speak to the people affected by a problem to gather real insight rather than guessing.

Define: the second half of the first diamond. Teams make sense of the discovery insights and reframe or clarify the challenge, moving from problem identification to a sharper problem definition.

Develop: the first half of the second diamond. Teams generate a diverse range of potential answers to the clearly defined problem, seeking inspiration from elsewhere and co-designing with a range of different people.

Deliver: the second half of the second diamond. Solutions are tested at small scale, the ones that do not work are rejected, and the ones that do are improved and refined.

## Divergent and convergent thinking

Each diamond widens then narrows. The first diamond diverges to explore the problem space broadly and converges to define the right problem. The second diamond diverges to explore many solutions and converges to deliver the ones that work. A core lesson of the model is that time must be spent understanding the problem before jumping to solutions.

## Evolution

The Design Council later expanded the model into the Framework for Innovation, adding design principles and methods and recognizing that the process is iterative and that ideas may never be truly finished. IDEO's Tim Brown characterized the framework as an invitation to get involved rather than a prescriptive manual.

title: Nielsen Norman Group, The Art of the Design Critique
text:
## Design critiques

A design critique is analyzing a design and providing feedback on whether it meets its objectives. It is a group conversation aimed at improving the work, not merely judging it. Critiques differ from design reviews, which evaluate work against heuristics, typically done by usability experts or at the conclusion of a creative process for approval.

## Roles

The presenter shares the design work. The critiquers offer informed perspectives against the stated objectives.

## Three themes of effective critiques

Effective critiques share three underlying themes: a clear conversation scope with unambiguous boundaries; agreed-upon design objectives for the work so feedback is measured against goals rather than taste; and conversation rather than command, meaning critiquers avoid directives that shut down open discussion.

## Facilitation techniques

Round robin: participants share perspectives sequentially so everyone contributes rather than a few dominating. Quotas: the facilitator gathers a predetermined number of positive and negative comments, for example two strengths and one area to improve. The facilitator creates and distributes the scope and agenda, asks clarifying questions that reframe subjective opinions back toward the design goals, documents the discussion, and follows up with notes and action items.

## Presenter best practices

Reiterate the objectives and personas beforehand, tell the story of the design, present quickly and efficiently to avoid overexplaining, and make the designs readily available.

## Anti-patterns to avoid

Not establishing personas or objectives before the critique; scheduling overly lengthy sessions; taking feedback personally; rushing to solve problems on the spot; and focusing exclusively on negatives instead of also naming what works.

title: Nielsen Norman Group, UX Prototypes: Low Fidelity vs. High Fidelity
text:
## Prototype fidelity

Fidelity describes how closely a prototype matches the look and feel of the final system. Fidelity is not a single slider but varies across three independent dimensions, so a prototype can be high fidelity on one dimension and low on another.

## Three dimensions of fidelity

Interactivity: high-fidelity interactivity means clickable links and menus with automatic responses to the user's actions, while low-fidelity interactivity uses non-functional targets where a facilitator delivers responses in real time (the human plays the computer).

Visuals: high-fidelity visuals show realistic visual hierarchy, priority of screen elements, and screen size, while low-fidelity visuals are sketches, wireframes, or schematics with minimal visual detail.

Content and navigation: high fidelity uses complete content matching the final design, while low fidelity uses summarized content or placeholder imagery.

## When to use each

High-fidelity prototypes produce faster, more realistic system responses; test specific UI components, workflow, and visual elements; often look like live software to users; reduce human error; and free the designer to observe testing. Low-fidelity prototypes are faster to prepare so they leave more time for iteration, are easier to modify mid-test, put less pressure on users because it is clear the design is being tested and not the person, and make designers feel less wedded to a given solution. Choose fidelity based on the timeline, how complete the design is, and the testing goal.

title: Nielsen Norman Group, Design Systems 101
text:
## Design systems

A design system is a complete set of standards intended to manage design at scale using reusable components and patterns. Its purpose is to operationalize design work across an organization managing many screens and products, treating the system itself as a living product with its own team, roadmap, and users (the designers and developers who consume it).

## Key components

Style guide: establishes visual and interaction standards, covering branding elements such as colors, typography, and logos, alongside content guidance like tone of voice and front-end specifications.

Component library: a repository of reusable UI elements documented with names, descriptions, attributes, states, code snippets, and implementation frameworks so designers and developers share one vocabulary and avoid miscommunication.

Pattern library: collections of grouped UI elements, layouts, and templates meant to be reused and adapted, distinct from individual component specs.

## Benefits

Design systems let teams rapidly replicate and scale design work, free designers to tackle complex problems instead of visual tweaking, establish shared vocabulary across teams, ensure visual consistency across products and channels, and serve as an educational resource for junior contributors.

## Implementation and governance

Organizations can adopt an existing system (lowest cost), adapt one to their needs, or build a proprietary system (highest investment); custom is warranted only when needs exceed open-source options. Effective systems require a dedicated team of interaction designers, visual designers, and developers, ideally with researchers, architects, and content writers, plus executive sponsorship. NN/g distinguishes a centralized model (one team builds and governs) from a distributed model (many contributors), each with trade-offs in speed and consistency.

title: IDEO, Design Thinking (Tim Brown)
text:
## IDEO's definition of design thinking

IDEO characterizes design thinking as a human-centered approach to innovation that draws from the designer's toolkit to integrate the needs of people, the possibilities of technology, and the requirements for business success. This is former CEO Tim Brown's canonical definition. The method synthesizes three overlapping considerations: what people find desirable, what is technologically feasible, and what is economically viable for the organization to sustain.

## Desirability, feasibility, viability

Innovative solutions live at the intersection of these three lenses. Design thinking deliberately starts from desirability, the human need, rather than from technical or financial constraints, and then works to make the desirable also feasible and viable. Solutions that ignore any one lens tend to fail: desirable but not feasible ideas cannot be built, and feasible but undesirable ones nobody wants.

## Process and mindset

IDEO frames design thinking as a flexible, iterative process rather than a rigid sequence, drawing on designers' mindsets to navigate uncertainty, generate new ideas, and learn by making and testing. The intent is not to turn everyone into designers but to help teams work more creatively and collaboratively. IDEO U is the organization's online school for developing these design-thinking and creative-leadership skills.

title: IDEO U, What Is Human-Centered Design?
text:
## Human-centered design

IDEO U describes human-centered design (HCD) as a creative approach to problem-solving that puts people, meaning users, customers, and stakeholders, at the heart of the process. The defining stance is designing with people, not just for them.

## Three overlapping phases

Inspiration: immerse in people's lives through observation, storytelling, and inquiry to uncover deep insights.

Ideation: translate insights into opportunities through brainstorming, rapid prototyping, and quick user testing.

Implementation: refine concepts, develop business models, and establish scaling strategies with long-term measurement.

These three phases can be broken into seven design-thinking steps, and they are not always linear: the process continuously loops back and iterates.

## Core mindsets

The methodology rests on mindsets that guide behavior throughout: empathy (understanding people's lives, emotions, motivations, and contexts); curiosity (staying open through bold questioning); embracing ambiguity (treating uncertainty as fertile ground); humility (listening openly and resisting bias); iteration (testing, learning from failure, refining); collaboration (co-creating with diverse expertise); optimism (assuming improvement is possible); and systems thinking (considering how a solution interacts with broader economic, cultural, and ecological systems).

## Mindset vs. toolkit

IDEO U frames HCD as the mindset and design thinking as the toolkit: a structured, iterative process that expresses the broader human-centered philosophy.

title: Nielsen Norman Group, Personas vs. Jobs-to-Be-Done
text:
## Jobs-to-Be-Done

Jobs-to-Be-Done (JTBD) is a framework based on the idea that whenever users hire (that is, use) a product, they do it for a specific job, meaning to achieve a particular outcome. JTBD is a representation of user needs born out of qualitative user research such as field studies, interviews, and discount usability testing.

## How JTBD differs from task analysis and use cases

The core differentiator between JTBD and traditional system-analysis techniques is that JTBD is much less prescriptive about what exactly the user's task is and how they will accomplish it. Task analysis and use cases aim to understand the best way for a product to handle typical activities, whereas JTBD moves the focus to desired outcomes and questions whether those typical activities are even the right way of reaching the outcomes users really seek.

## The structure of a job

A job statement typically captures what the user needs to accomplish, the context (why and where they do it), functional success criteria (the objective requirements), and emotional success criteria (personal and social considerations). Framing needs as outcomes keeps the team from locking in on one particular solution too early.

## Complementary, not competing

Well-crafted personas incorporate the same goal information as JTBD but add attitudinal, contextual, behavioral, and personal data. The two are quite compatible: personas help distinguish between different user groups with competing needs, while JTBD articulates the specific outcomes each is trying to achieve. Using them together gives both the who and the why.

title: Nielsen Norman Group, Minimize Design Risk by Focusing on Outcomes, Not Features
text:
## Outcomes vs. outputs

An output is a product or service that you create. An outcome is the problem that the product solves. One of the biggest traps in product planning is focusing on outputs over outcomes, that is, discussing what to build before clearly defining its purpose. Despite growing design awareness, many apps and websites fail because they solve problems that nobody cares about.

## Feature vs. benefit

The distinction parallels the classic marketing difference between a feature and a benefit. A feature is what a product offers; a benefit is what the customer actually wants. As in persuasive writing, you sell more by emphasizing a product's benefits instead of its features.

## Examples

For a B2B website, an output could be whitepapers and demonstration videos; the outcome could be knowledge gained by the customer. A cautionary example: a health-insurance website offering recipe content and a fitness tracker is a feasible output, but it misaligns with users who came for health-coverage information, not cooking tips.

## Why it reduces risk

A wonderful interface to the wrong features will fail even when execution is excellent. The safeguard is to know the customer problem before deciding how to solve it, so effort is spent on the outcome users care about rather than on polishing the wrong output.

title: Nielsen Norman Group, Empathy Mapping: The First Step in Design Thinking
text:
## Empathy mapping

An empathy map is a collaborative visualization used to articulate what a team knows about a particular type of user. Its dual purpose is to create shared understanding of user needs and to aid decision-making. Empathy maps are typically used early, in the empathize stage of design thinking, but remain useful from a design's inception through completion.

## The four quadrants

Says: direct quotes from research interviews or studies, what users verbalize about their experience.

Thinks: what occupies the user's mind but may go unspoken due to uncertainty, self-consciousness, or fear.

Does: the physical actions and behaviors users perform to accomplish tasks.

Feels: emotional states expressed as adjectives with context, such as worries, excitement, and overall sentiment.

## The process

A six-step process: define scope and goals (which user or persona and why); gather materials such as a whiteboard, sticky notes, or a digital tool; collect qualitative research (interviews, field studies, diary studies); generate individual sticky notes per quadrant; converge to cluster and synthesize findings collaboratively; and polish and plan for ongoing refinement as research evolves.

## Reading the map

Inconsistencies across quadrants, for example a user who says one thing but does another, reveal valuable insights. Empty quadrants signal insufficient research and where to dig next.

title: Nielsen Norman Group, Affinity Diagramming: Collaboratively Sort UX Findings and Design Ideas
text:
## Affinity diagramming

Affinity diagramming is the practice of organizing related observations, ideas, concepts, or findings into distinct clusters. It is also called affinity mapping, collaborative sorting, or snowballing, and it differs from card sorting, which is a specific research method for information architecture. It is a flexible activity used across UX stages, from synthesizing initial research through refining design.

## The three-step process

Step 1, generate ideas as sticky notes: team members independently write diverse ideas, observations, or data points on sticky notes in roughly 5 to 10 minutes and post them without particular order; independent contribution avoids groupthink in this divergent phase.

Step 2, organize notes into clusters or themes: look for sticky notes that reference similar ideas, issues, or functionality, group related items collaboratively, and give each cluster a clear label representing its content.

Step 3, prioritize clusters and next steps: the team ranks or votes on the clusters that matter most, using techniques like dot voting when consensus is hard, and designates point persons for accountability.

## Outcome

Successful affinity diagramming produces team alignment, robust design ideas, and a concrete set of next steps that move the project forward. It converts a scattered pile of raw observations into shared, prioritized themes.

title: Nielsen Norman Group, Personas: Study Guide
text:
## Personas

A persona is a fictional, yet realistic, description of a typical or target user of a product. Personas promote empathy, increase awareness and memorability of target users, help prioritize features, and inform design decisions by keeping a concrete user in mind throughout development.

## Three types by rigor

Lightweight (proto) personas: minimal effort, often assumption-based, useful as a starting point. Qualitative personas: grounded in qualitative user research, the most common and reliable type. Statistical personas: qualitative personas refined and validated with quantitative data.

## Related frameworks

The guide distinguishes personas from Jobs-to-Be-Done, a framework focused on outcomes, and from archetypes, a related but distinct way to represent users. Personas answer who and why in human terms; the others emphasize the job or the pattern.

## Applications

Personas feed scenario mapping and design ideation, feature prioritization, analytics segmentation, agile workflows, and research-participant recruitment. Primary and secondary personas help teams decide whose needs take precedence when they conflict.

## Maintenance and failure

Personas are not static; they need revision as the product and users change. A companion article, Why Personas Fail, catalogs the common mistakes, chief among them creating personas that are never actually used.

title: Nielsen Norman Group, Wireflows: A UX Deliverable for Workflows and Apps
text:
## Wireflows

A wireflow is a design-specification format that combines wireframe-style page-layout designs with a simplified flowchart-like way of representing interactions. It merges the what-the-screen-looks-like of a wireframe with the step-by-step task logic of a flowchart.

## When to use wireflows

Wireflows are most effective for mobile and web apps that have relatively few pages but change content dynamically, where selecting filters, facets, or interactive elements alters the page layout without a full navigation, and where interactions trigger AJAX or similar technologies. They suit ecommerce checkout flows and shopping-cart designs and any task where you must visualize system feedback in response to user actions. They work less well for traditional websites made of many discrete, relatively static pages linked sequentially, where a plain site map or flowchart is enough.

## How they combine elements

From wireframes, wireflows borrow actual screen designs that show layout, content, and visual context rather than abstract boxes. From flowcharts, they borrow step-by-step documentation with arrows indicating the specific UI component the user interacts with. Each node shows how the page appears after an action: changed content, a color change, a confirmation popup, or an error message. This lets the team see both what users see and how the interface responds.

title: Nielsen Norman Group, Minimum Viable Product (MVP): Definition
text:
## What an MVP is

A minimum viable product (MVP) is the simplest version of a product or feature that enables a team to assess whether users will derive meaningful value from it. It functions as an experiment to gather feedback before committing to full-scale investment.

## MVP as experiment, not launch

An MVP is a structured experiment, not a stripped-down product launch. That framing changes the optimization target: the goal is to sharpen the question the experiment answers rather than to polish features. Success requires a clear hypothesis and predetermined success criteria set before data collection begins.

## Usability still matters

A common misconception is that an MVP only needs to function. In reality, if an MVP is difficult to use, people may abandon it, not because the idea lacks value but because poor design obscures it. When usability is bad, the MVP becomes a test of the interface rather than a test of the idea.

## Anti-pattern: MVP is not Release 1

Teams often fail by building something minimal and treating the result as proof that the idea works or does not, when all they have really tested is whether people could use a rough interface. The MVP need not be the first public release; it can be a smaller, faster experiment whose only job is to reduce uncertainty about the core value proposition.

title: Nielsen Norman Group, Why Personas Fail (anti-patterns)
text:
## Why personas fail

Personas often fail not because the concept is flawed but because of how they are created and used. Nielsen Norman Group catalogs the recurring anti-patterns.

## Created but never used

Personas get developed but have no meaningful impact on projects. This is described as the largest barrier to future success: a failed first experience causes teams to dismiss personas as wasteful, which poisons future adoption.

## Lack of leadership buy-in

Decision-makers resist personas because they believe they already know their users well enough. Without executive support the initiative struggles for traction and resources.

## Siloed creation

Personas should not be an isolated endeavor undertaken by the UX team and unveiled like a piece of artwork. When stakeholders are not involved in creating them, they will not believe in or feel ownership of the results. Include the eventual persona users in the process to build investment.

## Communication breakdown

People do not understand what personas are or how to apply them. Personas are not 8.5 by 11 handouts; they must be actively woven into ongoing discussions and decisions through education and modeling.

## One-size-fits-all misuse

Personas are not a one-size-fits-all tool. When created for the wrong purpose or reused across different projects inappropriately, they fail to provide relevant, actionable insight for the work at hand.

title: Nielsen Norman Group, Usability Testing 101
text:
## Usability testing

Usability testing (user testing) is a research method in which a facilitator asks a participant to perform tasks using an interface while observing behavior and collecting feedback. Every usability test has three components: the facilitator (who gives tasks and observes), the tasks (realistic activities a real user might perform), and the participant (a realistic user of the product).

## Goals

The method identifies problems in the design of the product or service, uncovers opportunities to improve, and teaches the team about the target user's behavior and preferences.

## Qualitative vs. quantitative

Qualitative usability testing focuses on collecting insights, findings, and anecdotes about how people use the product; it is the more common form and is best for discovering problems. Quantitative usability testing emphasizes metrics such as task-success rate and time on task; it is best for benchmarking and answering how-many and how-much questions.

## How many participants

For a typical qualitative study of a single user group, five participants uncover the majority of the most common problems.

## Modalities

Moderated remote testing has the facilitator and participant interact through screen-sharing software in real time. Unmoderated remote testing has participants complete tasks independently in an online tool, and researchers review the recordings afterward.

## Think-aloud

In the think-aloud method, participants narrate their actions and thoughts as they work, which reveals behaviors, goals, thoughts, and motivations that would otherwise stay hidden. Common quantitative metrics include task-success rate, time on task, and error counts.

title: Jakob Nielsen, Nielsen Norman Group, Why You Only Need to Test with 5 Users
text:
## The 5-user rule

Jakob Nielsen and Tom Landauer's research established a model for how many usability problems a test uncovers. The number of problems found in a test with n users is:

N(1 - (1 - L)^n)

where N is the total number of usability problems in the design and L is the proportion of problems discovered by a single user, typically about 31 percent (0.31).

## Why five is enough

With L at 31 percent, testing with five users reveals approximately 85 percent of the usability problems in an interface. Zero users give zero insight. The first user alone provides almost a third of what there is to learn. Each additional user finds fewer new problems because observations start to repeat, and after about the fifth user you are wasting your time observing the same findings again.

## Iterate instead of over-testing (anti-pattern)

Rather than running one big study with 15 users, spend that budget on three studies with five users each. The first round of five finds about 85 percent of problems; you fix them, then the second round finds most of what remains and verifies the fixes, and the third round uncovers deeper issues exposed by the redesign. Iterative testing across multiple small rounds beats a single large test.

## Distinct user groups

When a product serves several highly distinct groups of users, test more: about 3 to 4 users per group for two groups, or about 3 users per group when there are three or more distinct groups.

title: Nielsen Norman Group, Card Sorting: Uncover Users' Mental Models for Better Information Architecture
text:
## Card sorting

Card sorting is a research method in which study participants place individually labeled cards into groups according to criteria that make the most sense to them. It uncovers users' mental models so teams can build an information architecture that matches how people naturally categorize content, improving findability.

## Three variations

Open card sort: participants create and name their own groups with no predefined categories, revealing natural categorization patterns. Closed card sort: researchers provide predefined categories and participants sort cards into them, typically to validate an existing structure. Hybrid card sort: some predefined categories plus the option to add new ones; generally discouraged because it can bias results.

## Practical parameters

Use roughly 30 to 50 cards to prevent participant fatigue while still encouraging thoughtful grouping. For qualitative insight into the reasoning behind groupings, use at least 15 participants; for quantitative, generalizable results use 30 to 50 participants. Remote studies using tools like OptimalSort are more common than in-person sessions and offer automated analysis.

## Limitations

Card sorting isolates content items from the contextual cues (images, structure, links) that influence real navigation, and it usually produces single-level groupings rather than a full hierarchy. It suggests groupings but does not by itself hand you the exact categorization scheme to ship, which is why it is paired with tree testing.

title: Nielsen Norman Group, Tree Testing
text:
## Tree testing

Tree testing is the evaluation of a hierarchical category structure, or tree, by having users find where in the tree specific resources or features live. It needs only two things: the hierarchical menu shown as expandable text (without visual design), and task instructions telling participants what to locate. Because there is no visual design, it isolates the labels and structure themselves.

## Card sorting vs. tree testing

Card sorting is generative: it discovers possible groupings by having users organize content, capturing mental models but not proving that people can find things. Tree testing is evaluative: it tests whether users can actually locate resources within a proposed hierarchy. Card sorting does not usually produce the exact categorization scheme you should follow, whereas tree testing directly measures findability performance.

## Metrics

Tree testing captures success rate (did users reach the correct answer), directness (did they go straight there or backtrack through several categories, signaling label confusion), time on task, and click patterns showing which categories users chose and thus alternative mental models.

## Where it fits

A typical IA research sequence is: usability test the current structure to find problems, run a card sort to generate redesign options, then run tree tests to assess one or more candidate hierarchies before design and development begin. This validates structural changes early, without creating needless churn and revisions.

title: Nielsen Norman Group, Journey Mapping 101
text:
## Journey mapping

A journey map is a visualization of the process that a person goes through in order to accomplish a goal. It compiles a user's actions into a timeline, enriches that timeline with the user's thoughts and emotions to create a narrative, and condenses the narrative into a visualization.

## Five key components

1. Actor: the persona or user who experiences the journey, one perspective per map, grounded in research; different user types need separate maps.

2. Scenario and expectations: the specific situation the map addresses, tied to the actor's goal or need and their expectations; scenarios can be real (existing product) or anticipated (future design).

3. Journey phases: the high-level stages that organize the experience, for example discover, try, buy, use, support for ecommerce.

4. Actions, mindsets, and emotions: the behaviors form a narrative rather than granular steps; mindsets capture the customer's verbatim thoughts; emotions are plotted as a line showing ups and downs across phases.

5. Opportunities: the insights about how to improve the experience, including who owns each change and how it will be measured.

## When to use it

Journey maps work best for experiences that span a sequence of events, transition over time, or cross multiple channels. They differ from experience maps (broader, product-agnostic), service blueprints (which extend the map into backstage business processes), and user-story maps (implementation-focused).

title: Christian Rohrer, Nielsen Norman Group, When to Use Which User-Experience Research Methods
text:
## A 3-dimensional framework for choosing methods

NN/g maps UX research methods along three dimensions so you can pick the right one for the question you have.

## Attitudinal vs. behavioral

This axis contrasts what people say (attitudinal) with what people do (behavioral); the two very often differ. Surveys and interviews capture attitudes; A/B testing and analytics capture behavior; usability studies and field studies blend both but lean behavioral.

## Qualitative vs. quantitative

Qualitative methods observe behavior or attitudes directly and are much better suited to answering why or how to fix a problem. Quantitative methods gather data indirectly through a measurement instrument and are much better at answering how-many and how-much questions.

## Context of use

Methods also differ by how participants use the product during the study: natural use (minimal interference, as in ethnographic field studies and intercept surveys), scripted use (focused on specific tasks, as in benchmarking), limited or decontextualized use (studying an abstracted aspect, as in card sorting or concept testing), and not using the product at all (studying broader issues like brand).

## Mapping and phases

Usability testing and interviews are behavioral or qualitative and scripted; surveys are attitudinal and quantitative; A/B testing and analytics are behavioral, quantitative, and natural. Methods should combine across product phases: generative (strategize), formative (execute and refine the design), and summative (assess against benchmarks or competitors).

title: Jakob Nielsen, Nielsen Norman Group, Severity Ratings for Usability Problems
text:
## Rating usability-problem severity

Severity helps teams prioritize which usability problems to fix first. Nielsen defines it as a combination of three factors: frequency (how common the problem is), impact (how hard it is for users to overcome), and persistence (whether it is a one-time nuisance or hits users repeatedly). A fourth consideration is market impact: some problems have an outsized effect on a product's appeal even if they seem technically easy to fix.

## The 0 to 4 severity scale

0 = I do not agree that this is a usability problem at all.
1 = Cosmetic problem only: need not be fixed unless extra time is available.
2 = Minor usability problem: fixing this should be given low priority.
3 = Major usability problem: important to fix, so it should be given high priority.
4 = Usability catastrophe: imperative to fix this before the product can be released.

## Using the ratings

Combine all severity factors into a single overall rating so problems can be ranked and triaged. Severity ratings are more reliable when gathered from multiple evaluators; the mean of a set of ratings from three evaluators is considered satisfactory for most practical purposes. Collect ratings after a heuristic evaluation is complete, not during, so evaluators first focus on finding problems.

title: Nielsen Norman Group, How to Conduct a Heuristic Evaluation
text:
## Heuristic evaluation

A heuristic evaluation is a method for identifying design problems in a user interface by having evaluators judge the design against established usability guidelines (heuristics). It is a form of discount usability: fast and cheap compared with full user testing.

## How many evaluators

The method works best with 3 to 5 independent evaluators rather than a single person, because different evaluators find different problems and one person misses too much. Each evaluator inspects the interface alone first, then findings are combined.

## Foundational heuristics

The recommended baseline is Jakob Nielsen's 10 usability heuristics, high-level principles grounded in human behavior; these can be supplemented with domain-specific heuristics for specialized contexts.

## Process

Prepare by reading the heuristics, running a practice round, deciding how to document findings, and narrowing scope by task, section, user group, or device. Each evaluator then spends roughly 1 to 2 hours independently reviewing: first getting familiar with the product, then systematically checking for violations of the heuristics. Finally the team consolidates, often via affinity diagramming, discussing agreement, severity, and priority for fixes.

## Strengths and the key limitation

Heuristic evaluation is cost-effective for catching obvious problems, useful early in design, and builds the team's UX intuition. Its critical limitation: heuristic evaluations cannot replace user research. Because design is contextual, actual user testing is still needed to confirm whether a flagged violation truly causes a problem for real users.

title: Nielsen Norman Group, Information Architecture: Study Guide
text:
## Information architecture

Information architecture (IA) is the underlying structure that organizes content; it is fundamentally different from navigation, which is the visible interface that presents that structure to users. Good IA rests on understanding how people seek information.

## Findability and information scent

IA distinguishes findability (users locating a known item) from discoverability (users stumbling on relevant content they were not specifically seeking). A central concept is information scent: users follow their noses through a hierarchy, judging at each step from labels and contextual clues whether a path leads toward what they want. Clear link labels carry strong scent; vague labels like Learn More carry weak scent.

## Organizational structures

Common structures include flat hierarchies (fewer levels, broader categories) and deep hierarchies (more levels, narrower categories), plus polyhierarchies, which cross-list an item under multiple categories to improve findability for ambiguous content. Categorization best practice pays special attention to outliers, items that do not fit neatly into any group.

## Research methods

IA has its own research methods that differ from other UX methods. Card sorting (open or closed) uncovers users' mental models to generate groupings. Tree testing evaluates a proposed hierarchy by measuring whether users can efficiently locate key items, with results often examined through dendrogram analysis. The two are complementary: card sorting generates structures, tree testing validates them before build.

title: W3C Web Accessibility Initiative, Accessibility Principles (POUR)
text:
## The POUR principles

The W3C Web Accessibility Initiative (WAI) organizes the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) requirements around four principles, remembered as POUR: Perceivable, Operable, Understandable, Robust.

## Perceivable

Information and interface components must be presentable in ways users can perceive. This includes text alternatives (equivalents) for non-text content such as images, charts, audio, and video; captions and audio descriptions for multimedia; content that is adaptable because headings, lists, tables, input fields, and structure are marked up properly; and distinguishable content with sufficient color contrast, resizable text, and controllable audio. (WCAG guidelines 1.1 to 1.4.)

## Operable

Interface and navigation must be operable. All functionality available by mouse must also be available by keyboard; users need enough time to read and use content and the ability to pause moving elements; content must not flash in ways that can cause seizures; navigation must be clear with descriptive headings and multiple ways to find pages; and input beyond keyboard (touch, voice) should be supported. (WCAG guidelines 2.1 to 2.5.)

## Understandable

Information and operation must be understandable. Text should be readable, with the page's primary language identified and unusual terms defined; interfaces should be predictable, with consistent navigation and labeling; and input assistance should provide descriptive instructions, error messages, and suggestions for correction. (WCAG guidelines 3.1 to 3.3.)

## Robust

Content must be robust enough to be interpreted reliably by a wide range of user agents, including assistive technologies, for example by ensuring markup is valid. (WCAG guideline 4.1.)

title: Jeff Sauro, MeasuringU, Measuring Usability with the System Usability Scale (SUS)
text:
## System Usability Scale (SUS)

The SUS was developed by John Brooke in 1986 as a quick and dirty scale for post-test usability assessment. It has become an industry standard referenced in hundreds of publications.

## The questionnaire

The SUS is 10 statements, each rated on a 5-point Likert scale from Strongly disagree to Strongly agree. Items alternate between positive and negative wording (odd items positive, even items negative) and cover things like perceived complexity, ease of use, need for support, consistency, and confidence.

## Scoring

To score: for each odd-numbered item subtract 1 from the user's response; for each even-numbered item subtract the response from 5. Sum these converted scores (range 0 to 40) and multiply by 2.5 to get a SUS score on a 0 to 100 scale.

## Interpretation

A SUS score is NOT a percentage, even though it ranges 0 to 100. The average SUS score across a large set of studies is 68, which sits at roughly the 50th percentile. Scores above 68 are above average and below 68 are below average. Scores convert to percentile ranks and letter grades (A+ through F) using a curve: for example a raw score of about 74 is near the 70th percentile (about a B-), and a score of 80.3 or higher earns an A. Because a 70 is only about the 50th percentile, converting to percentiles is important when communicating results to stakeholders.

title: Jon Yablonski, Laws of UX, Hick's Law
text:
## Hick's Law

The time it takes to make a decision increases with the number and complexity of choices. The principle is named for psychologists William Edmund Hick and Ray Hyman, who in 1952 examined the relationship between the number of stimuli present and a person's reaction time; reaction time grows logarithmically as the number of choices increases.

## Takeaways for design

Minimize choices when response times are critical, so the decision is faster. Break complex tasks into smaller steps to decrease cognitive load. Avoid overwhelming users by highlighting recommended or preferred options. Use progressive onboarding to ease new users in gradually. But do not oversimplify to the point of abstracting away meaningful functionality; hiding needed capability is its own failure.

## Examples

Google's homepage strips away distractions to focus attention on a single search input. Apple TV remotes push interface complexity onto the screen, allowing features to be revealed progressively. Slack's onboarding reveals capabilities over time rather than dumping every feature on a newcomer at once.

title: Jon Yablonski, Laws of UX, Miller's Law
text:
## Miller's Law

The average person can only keep about 7 (plus or minus 2) items in their working memory. In 1956 psychologist George Miller found that both immediate memory span and one-dimensional absolute judgment were limited to roughly 7 units of information. Miller defined the basic unit of information as the bit, the amount of data needed to decide between two equally probable alternatives.

## Takeaways for design

Do not use the magical number seven to justify unnecessary design limits; the number is often misapplied as a hard rule for menu items or list lengths, which was not Miller's claim. Instead, use chunking: organize content into smaller, meaningful groups so users can process, understand, and remember it more easily (phone numbers grouped into segments are the classic example). Remember that working-memory capacity varies from person to person depending on prior knowledge and situational context.

## Key concept: chunking

Chunking restructures how information is presented, grouping it into unified, meaningful segments rather than simply reducing the total amount. It works with the mind's limits rather than against them.

title: Jon Yablonski, Laws of UX, Jakob's Law
text:
## Jakob's Law

Users spend most of their time on other sites. This means that users prefer your site to work the same way as all the other sites they already know. The law is named for Jakob Nielsen, principal of Nielsen Norman Group (co-founded with Don Norman), who established the discount usability engineering movement and invented methods including heuristic evaluation.

## Takeaways for design

Users transfer expectations they have built around one familiar product to another that looks similar, so leaning on established conventions lets users focus on their task rather than on learning a new model. By leveraging existing mental models you create better experiences with less friction. When you must make changes, minimize dissonance by letting users continue to use a familiar version for a limited time.

## Example

YouTube's 2017 redesign let users preview the new Material Design interface, give feedback, and switch back to the old version, which reduced the friction of the transition and respected users' existing mental models.

title: Nielsen Norman Group, Top 10 Application-Design Mistakes (anti-patterns)
text:
## Top application-design mistakes (anti-patterns)

Nielsen Norman Group's list of common application UI mistakes doubles as a checklist of what not to do.

1. Poor feedback: failing to show system state, how a command was interpreted, or progress for slow operations, so users cannot tell what is happening.

2. Inconsistency: differing terminology for the same action, controls placed in different spots, and unpredictable feature availability; differences are hard for users.

3. Bad error messages: messages that do not explain the cause or how to recover, like a vague Something went wrong.

4. No default values: omitting sensible defaults forces users to specify values they should not have to.

5. Unlabeled icons: nonstandard icons without text labels create guessing and confusion.

6. Hard-to-acquire targets: weak signifiers and tiny click zones make targets hard to hit, hurting older users and those with motor impairments (a Fitts's Law problem).

7. Overuse of modals: modal windows cover context the user may need while filling a form or editing data.

8. Meaningless information: showing database IDs or encoded codes instead of human-readable content raises cognitive load.

9. Junk-drawer menus: overflow menus labeled More, Tools, or an ellipsis lack information scent and hide features.

10. Proximity of destructive and confirming actions: placing Save and Delete or similar opposing controls close together invites accidental, irreversible clicks.

title: Harry Brignull, Deceptive Design, Types of Deceptive Patterns (anti-patterns)
text:
## Deceptive (dark) patterns

Deceptive patterns, originally coined dark patterns by Harry Brignull, are design choices that mislead or manipulate users into doing things against their own interest through hidden information, misdirection, or coercion. The site catalogs a taxonomy of named types; recognizing them is a core ethical competency for UX designers.

## Named types

Forced action: the user wants to do something but is required to do something else undesirable in return. Sneaking: the user is drawn into a transaction on false pretenses because pertinent information is hidden or delayed. Hard to cancel: easy to sign up but very hard to cancel (also called roach motel). Preselection: a default option is pre-checked to steer the decision. Obstruction: barriers or hurdles are placed to make a task, such as cancelling, harder than it should be. Hidden costs: a low price is shown until unexpected fees appear at checkout. Hidden subscription: the user is enrolled in recurring charges without clear disclosure. Trick wording: confusing or misleading language, such as double negatives. Visual interference: important information is hidden, obscured, or disguised. Fake social proof, fake urgency, and fake scarcity: false claims about popularity, time limits, or stock to pressure a decision. Nagging: persistent repeated requests to do something the user keeps declining. Confirmshaming: emotional manipulation, wording the decline option to shame the user. Comparison prevention, disguised ads, and currency confusion round out the catalog.

## Why it matters

Deceptive patterns can boost short-term conversion but erode trust, damage brand, and increasingly violate consumer-protection law and privacy regulation. Ethical UX designers use persuasion transparently and let users make informed choices.
